title: SRE Fundamentals
summary: What Site Reliability Engineering actually is as a discipline, and how it differs from traditional ops and from "DevOps" as a buzzword.

slides.markdown:
**Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)** is what you get when software engineers design and run production operations, instead of a separate team following runbooks by hand.

- The core belief: an ops problem is a **software problem** — automate it, don't just document it.
- The central metric is **toil**: manual, repetitive work that adds no lasting value.
- SRE overlaps with DevOps but is a specific, more prescriptive implementation of it.

slides.subTitle: "What happens when a software engineer runs production"
slides.markdown:
Google's Ben Treynor Sloss, who coined the term, defined SRE as **"what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations function."** Rather than a separate ops team executing runbooks manually, SREs write software to solve operational problems — monitoring, deploy automation, capacity planning, incident response.

The practical consequence: if the same page fires three times, the fix isn't a clearer runbook step — it's code that detects and resolves the condition automatically, so a human never gets paged for it again.

slides.subTitle: Engineering the fix vs applying it
slides.markdown:
| | Traditional sysadmin ops | SRE |
|---|---|---|
| Response to a recurring failure | Follow/update a runbook | Write code to eliminate the failure mode |
| Skill bar | Operational, tool-driven | Software engineering + operations |
| Success measure | Uptime, tickets closed | Toil trending down, SLOs met |
| Scaling model | Hire more people as load grows | Automation absorbs the growth |

Both care about keeping systems up — SRE just refuses to let "keeping it up" stay a manual job forever.

slides.subTitle: Overlapping, not identical
slides.markdown:
**DevOps** is a cultural philosophy: break down the wall between dev and ops, ship faster and safer together. It doesn't prescribe *how*.

**SRE** is one concrete implementation of that philosophy, with specific mechanisms: error budgets, SLOs, blameless postmortems, a toil cap, and treating ops work as a software engineering discipline.

A useful line: **"SRE is what happens when you implement DevOps with a software engineer's mindset and a specific set of practices."** You can do DevOps without SRE's exact tooling; you can't do SRE without DevOps's underlying philosophy.

**Toil** is work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and produces no lasting engineering value — it scales linearly with the system, not sub-linearly. Restarting a crashed service by hand every night is toil; the code that detects the crash and restarts it automatically is engineering.

Not all manual work is toil — a one-off migration or a novel investigation isn't toil, because it isn't repetitive. The test is: **would doing this again next week look identical?** If yes, it's a candidate for automation, not a permanent job.

slides.sectionTitle: Why reducing toil is the core lever
slides.markdown:
Toil doesn't just cost time — it **compounds against you**. As a service grows, manual operational work grows with it; without deliberate reduction, an SRE team eventually spends 100% of its time just keeping the lights on, with zero capacity left to improve reliability further.

Google's SRE model caps ops-style work at roughly **50%** of an SRE's time — the rest is protected for engineering that reduces future toil. That cap is a forcing function: it makes "automate this" a scheduled priority instead of something perpetually deferred for the next fire.

slides.subTitle: A runbook becomes self-healing
slides.markdown:
A service leaks memory and OOMs roughly weekly. Month one: the on-call runbook says "SSH in, restart the process." That's pure toil — same steps, same outcome, forever.

An SRE instead adds a **liveness probe** that detects the memory threshold and restarts the process automatically, then files a ticket to fix the underlying leak. The page volume for this issue drops to zero without anyone touching a terminal at 3am. The runbook didn't get better — it got **deleted**, replaced by code.

slides.subTitle: The gate before SRE takes the pager
slides.markdown:
Many SRE orgs don't accept every service that asks for support — they gate it behind a **Production Readiness Review (PRR)**: a checklist covering defined SLOs, working monitoring and alerting, written runbooks, a load test at expected scale, and a rollback that's actually been exercised, not just documented.

A service that fails the PRR doesn't get SRE support yet — the development team keeps carrying its own pager until the gaps close. The point isn't gatekeeping for its own sake: accepting an unready service without a means to measure or bound its operational load just imports someone else's toil wholesale, with no lever to reduce it.

slides.subTitle: SRE in name only
slides.markdown:
A common anti-pattern: a company renames its ops team "SRE" without adopting the mechanisms that make SRE actually work — no error budgets that gate launches, no toil cap that's enforced, no protected engineering time. The team keeps doing 100% firefighting under a new title, and nothing structurally changes.

A quick tell: ask "when's the last time a launch was actually blocked by an exhausted error budget?" If the honest answer is never, the SLOs are decorative — numbers on a dashboard with no real policy enforcing them, which is a title change, not the discipline SRE is supposed to be.
